scenes.title: Key ideas
scenes.vo: You don't need to be a developer to spot the things that matter. In verified Solidity code on an explorer, look for: First, Access control: onlyOwner, onlyRole(...), onlyGovernance. Who can call what? Search for functions guarded by them. Next, Dangerous powers: mint, pause, upgradeTo, setOracle, setFee, withdraw/sweep/rescue functions that move user funds. Then, Upgradeability: proxy patterns (delegatecall, implementation, upgradeTo), and who the admin is (5.4). Also, External calls and state order: calling another contract before updating balances is the classic reentrancy pattern (5.5). On top of that, Parameters with no limits: a fee that can be set to 100%, or an oracle address that can be swapped instantly.

scenes.title: Worked example
steps: Check the owner() value on the Read tab.
scenes.vo: Let's work an example, step by step. A token claims "fixed supply". In its code you find: The owner can mint unlimited tokens: the claim is false unless ownership is renounced or held by a timelocked governance contract. Check the owner() value on the Read tab.

scenes.title: Checklist
items: Searched the code for owner/role-guarded functions

Checked who holds those roles (Read tab) and behind what timelock

scenes.q: What does onlyOwner on a mint function mean?
scenes.a: The owner can mint new tokens whenever they like.

scenes.q: What code pattern suggests reentrancy risk?
scenes.a: An external call made before the contract updates its own state.
